source_family: Two families: (1) github.com/ariga/atlas issue and pull-request tracker, queried directly via the GitHub REST Search API (api.github.com/search/issues) rather than a general web search engine, giving an authoritative, exhaustive-within-query result set rather than a search-engine's partial index; (2) atlasgo.io/concepts/dev-database, the official documentation page describing the dev-database requirement — distinct from, but maintained by the same org as, the atlasgo.io pages used in the sibling licence-governance and other Atlas HCL facet records.
precise_evidence_location: api.github.com/search/issues queries scoped to repo:ariga/atlas for: composite primary key, self reference foreign key, multiple schemas, enum, unique constraint, nullable foreign key, custom lint rule, dev database required, and 'is not supported' in:title; individual issues github.com/ariga/atlas/issues/1584, /2957, /2180, /1614, /1551, /2086, /2252, and pull request github.com/ariga/atlas/pull/417; atlasgo.io/concepts/dev-database (full page).
method: Direct, unauthenticated calls to the public GitHub REST Search API (via curl, parsed with jq) against repo:ariga/atlas for each of the ten advanced constructs plus validator/live-connection/product-neutrality terms, reading total_count, issue/PR number, state, title, and (for the most relevant hits) the full issue body via a follow-up direct GET to api.github.com/repos/ariga/atlas/issues/<n>. This is a stronger method than a general web search engine, per the limitation the sibling source-linkml-contrary-evidence.json record flagged for LinkML's equivalent search (it recommended exactly this API-based approach as the improvement). One official documentation page (atlasgo.io/concepts/dev-database) was also fetched directly, since search_angle 9 also covers 'documented limitations' and 'capabilities that require a live database connection', which is a documented-behaviour question rather than an issue-tracker question.
limitations: The GitHub Search API's unauthenticated rate limit is 10 requests/minute, which constrained the number of distinct construct-specific queries run in one pass; some queries (e.g. 'one-to-zero-or-one relationship', 'domain_id convention') have no natural issue-tracker vocabulary and were not separately queried because no plausible search term was identified — this is recorded as a genuine search-method gap for those two constructs, not as a confirmed absence of relevant issues. Search was title/body full-text matching (`in:title,body`), which will miss issues using materially different terminology (e.g. 'compound key' rather than 'composite key', or discussion in a closed PR review thread rather than an issue). Several queries returned issues about migration-time bugs (ALTER-time behaviour) rather than initial-schema-expressibility gaps; these are recorded and classified separately from expressibility, consistent with the distinction the plan's research questions draw between 'expressible' and the CLI's actual validate/apply/lint behaviour. The dev-database finding describes an ephemeral, Docker-driven database instance, not a persistent live database — this record is precise about that distinction rather than overstating it as 'Atlas requires a live production database connection'.
provenance: Retrieved 2026-08-14 via curl against api.github.com/search/issues and api.github.com/repos/ariga/atlas/issues/<n> (public, unauthenticated GitHub REST API, subject to GitHub's published rate limits — reset time and remaining quota observed via api.github.com/rate_limit during this pass) and via WebFetch against https://atlasgo.io/concepts/dev-database. several_logical_schemas_in_one_database_.citation: ariga/atlas#1584 (open, silent no-op when applying multiple HCL schema files together); ariga/atlas#2957 (open, same-named tables across schema files collide with 'multiple reference tables found' unless every table is written with the qualified table "<schema>" "<name>" form)
several_logical_schemas_in_one_database_.rationale: This directly contradicts a reading of the sibling source-atlas-hcl-hcl-language.json record's 'expressible' classification for multiple logical schemas as friction-free: that record correctly documents the Table-Qualification mechanism exists, but this contrary-evidence pass found two open, still-unresolved issues showing the mechanism is not merely an optional style choice — omitting it produces either a hard error ('multiple reference tables found') or, worse, a silent no-op where `schema apply` reports no changes despite a genuine multi-schema diff (#1584, open since 2023, no fix confirmed as of this search). For Gigacron's actual case — the configuration/runtime/audit/resources split named in ADR-0001, which per the arc42 system map places tables with identical or overlapping names in different logical schemas — this is exactly the collision scenario #2957 reproduces. The construct remains classified expressible-only-via-workaround, but this record adds that the workaround (universal, disciplined use of qualified table names across every multi-schema HCL project) is not optional in practice and that at least one related bug (#1584) is open and unresolved, not merely a historical/closed defect.

capabilities_requiring_a_live_database_e.citation: atlasgo.io/concepts/dev-database: 'Parsing schemas and migrations is not enough... only the real engine, with the right version and extensions, can compile every expression, resolve every reference, and accept the result'; docker:// driver syntax for an ephemeral dev database
capabilities_requiring_a_live_database_e.rationale: This is a documented, official-source limitation, not an issue-tracker gap: for anything beyond bare syntax parsing — meaningful semantic validation, `schema apply`, `migrate diff`, `schema plan`, `schema lint` — Atlas requires a running instance of the actual target database engine (the 'dev database'), which Atlas can spin up as an ephemeral Docker container via the `docker://<engine>/<version>/<name>` driver rather than a persistent live database. This is precise: it is NOT a requirement for a persistent production database connection, but it IS a requirement heavier than 'work from the HCL file alone' — it requires Docker (or an external database) at validation time, and it requires committing to one specific database engine and version for that dev container, which reopens the product-neutrality question the brief's exclusions explicitly try to keep closed at the specification level ('the modeling language must stay product-neutral at the specification level'; ADR-0001 leaves the database product unchosen). A CI gate built on `atlas schema lint --dev-url docker://postgres/15/dev ...` is implicitly a PostgreSQL-flavoured gate, not a product-neutral one, even though the HCL schema syntax itself (per the sibling hcl-language.json and product-neutrality.json records) keeps its structural keywords dialect-neutral. This corroborates, from an independent official-docs source, the dialect-leak finding already recorded in source-atlas-hcl-product-neutrality.json, and extends it: the leak is not only at the type-name/check-expression level but also at the validator's own runtime dependency level.

check_value_constraint_dialect_and_versi.citation: ariga/atlas#417 (merged PR, 2022-01-15): 'sql/mysql: reject CHECK constraints when it is not supported by the database'
check_value_constraint_dialect_and_versi.rationale: This closes part of the open gap the sibling source-atlas-hcl-validation-exit.json record flagged ('No page found confirming or denying MySQL's version-gated CHECK-constraint enforcement... in the context of Atlas specifically'): Atlas does have code, merged in 2022, that specifically rejects (rather than silently accepts) CHECK constraints when targeting a MySQL version/configuration that does not enforce them. This is good CI-gate behaviour in one sense — a malformed-for-the-target-dialect CHECK constraint is caught rather than silently ignored — but it is also direct evidence that the CHECK/value-constraint-beyond-type construct's actual acceptance is dialect-and-version-dependent, not a uniform, product-neutral guarantee: the same HCL `check { expr = ... }` block that validates cleanly against one MySQL version/config can be rejected against another, and this determination requires the live dev-database engine described above, not the HCL file in isolation.

enum_construct_evolution_gap.citation: ariga/atlas#2252 (closed, 2023-11-04): 'Error: replacing or reordering enum value is not supported'
enum_construct_evolution_gap.rationale: The enumerated-string-domain construct is confirmed expressible for initial schema authoring (sibling source-atlas-hcl-hcl-language.json / hcl-types record). This issue is contrary evidence at the maintenance layer: once a PostgreSQL enum type exists, reordering or replacing its value set through Atlas's declarative/versioned migration flow hits a hard, explicitly-named 'not supported' error, requiring a manual workaround (typically a raw SQL migration step) outside the HCL-driven flow. Because Gigacron's FOLDER_RUN.execution_context and NAMED_RESOURCE_LINK.link_kind enums are exactly the kind of fixed-value-set construct this affects, this is recorded as a genuine gap between what the HCL language can express once and what the CLI's own migration tooling can evolve over time — directly answering the plan's 'gap between the HCL language and what the CLI actually validates or renders' angle.

composite_key_and_multi_column_unique_op.citation: ariga/atlas#1614 (closed, composite FK regenerated with duplicate constraint); ariga/atlas#1551 (closed, [BUG, postgres] failure dropping a field while changing a composite key, due to statement ordering); ariga/atlas#2086 (open, renaming a table with a UNIQUE CONSTRAINT fails because the new table is created before the old constraint is dropped)
composite_key_and_multi_column_unique_op.rationale: None of these dispute that composite primary keys or multi-column UNIQUE constraints can be DECLARED in HCL (both remain classified expressible in the sibling hcl-language.json record for initial authoring). They are contrary evidence at the migration-execution layer: composite keys and UNIQUE constraints have a real history of Atlas's own migration planner mis-ordering the generated DDL statements around them (drop-before-create races, duplicate-constraint regeneration). Two of the three are closed (presumed fixed); #2086 is open at time of search. Recorded as operational risk on top of, not instead of, the 'expressible' authoring-time classification.
